claim: Puttaswamy conclusion 3(C) and 3(B): privacy emerges primarily from the guarantee of life and personal liberty in Article 21, with elements arising from other freedoms in Part III; life and personal liberty are not creations of the Constitution but are recognised as inhering in each individual.
value: privacy rooted in Art 21 and Part III
source: K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India, 24 Aug 2017 (nine judges), Supreme Court official copy
note: Adds to ledger POL03-D12 (the Order of the Court).

claim: Puttaswamy conclusion 3(E): 'Privacy is the constitutional core of human dignity.'
source: K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India, 24 Aug 2017 (nine judges), Supreme Court official copy

claim: Puttaswamy conclusion 3(F): privacy includes at its core personal intimacies, the sanctity of family life, marriage, procreation, the home and sexual orientation, and a right to be left alone; it is not lost merely because a person is in a public place.
source: K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India, 24 Aug 2017 (nine judges), Supreme Court official copy
note: Procreation and family life are the heads closest to a paternity question.

claim: Puttaswamy conclusion 3(H): privacy is not absolute; a law invading it must satisfy legality, a legitimate State aim and proportionality (a rational nexus between object and means), with a fair, just and reasonable procedure.
source: K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India, 24 Aug 2017 (nine judges), Supreme Court official copy
note: Same as ledger POL03-D13. The Bhabani Prasad Jena Court (2010) used 'proportionality' for DNA tests before Puttaswamy; that is read through Firodia, not directly.

claim: Aparna Ajinkya Firodia (20 Feb 2023, Nagarathna and Ramasubramanian JJ.): the Supreme Court held that the Family Court and High Court were wrong to allow a husband's application to subject the child to a DNA test; the appeal was allowed, though the husband may lead other evidence of the wife's alleged infidelity.
source: Aparna Ajinkya Firodia v Ajinkya Arun Firodia, 20 Feb 2023 (Nagarathna and Ramasubramanian JJ.), Supreme Court official copy
page_or_section: Ramasubramanian J. concurring, final paras 36; PDF pp.71-72
note: The case is about a child already born, in a divorce petition on grounds of adultery. It is not about an unborn child.

claim: Firodia on Section 112 of the Evidence Act: birth of a child during a valid marriage, or within 280 days after its dissolution, is 'conclusive proof' of legitimacy unless it is shown that the spouses had no access to each other when the child could have been conceived; the burden is on the person who questions legitimacy.
source: Aparna Ajinkya Firodia v Ajinkya Arun Firodia, 20 Feb 2023 (Nagarathna and Ramasubramanian JJ.), Supreme Court official copy
note: The same page says the presumption 'can be rebutted only by strong, clear and conclusive evidence'. Note that s.112 turns on the time of birth, so it speaks of a child 'born'; the Court says time of conception matters only for the access test (para 8.2). [Audit 10 Nov 2026] Page corrected: s.112 rule and 280 days are on PDF p.18; burden on p.19.

claim: Goutam Kundu v State of West Bengal (1993) 3 SCC 418, as set out in Firodia: 'courts in India cannot order blood test as a matter of course'; no roving inquiry; a strong prima facie case of non-access is needed; the court must weigh whether the test would brand the child a bastard and the mother unchaste; no one can be compelled to give a sample.
source: Aparna Ajinkya Firodia v Ajinkya Arun Firodia, 20 Feb 2023 (Nagarathna and Ramasubramanian JJ.), Supreme Court official copy
note: Read through the Court's own quotation in Firodia. The 1993 judgment itself was not opened. [Audit 10 Nov 2026] Page corrected: the five principles (para 26 of Goutam Kundu) are on p.33.

claim: Bhabani Prasad Jena v Convenor Secretary, Orissa State Commission for Women, as summarised in Firodia: DNA profiling to decide paternity is 'an extremely delicate and sensitive aspect', to be directed only on 'eminent need', after weighing the s.112 presumption and the pros and cons, and only where there is a strong prima facie case.
source: Aparna Ajinkya Firodia v Ajinkya Arun Firodia, 20 Feb 2023 (Nagarathna and Ramasubramanian JJ.), Supreme Court official copy
note: The 3 Aug 2010 judgment (Lodha and Aftab Alam JJ.) was not opened at the Court's site; only the Court's own summary in Firodia is used.

claim: Sharda v Dharmpal (2003) 4 SCC 493, as applied in Firodia: a Family Court has power to direct a person to undergo medical tests, including a DNA test, and such an order does not violate the right to personal liberty under Article 21; but it should be passed only when expedient in the interest of justice, and 'not mechanically in each and every case'.
value: medical test not per se against Art 21
source: Aparna Ajinkya Firodia v Ajinkya Arun Firodia, 20 Feb 2023 (Nagarathna and Ramasubramanian JJ.), Supreme Court official copy
note: This is the Court's own bridge between privacy under Article 21 and a court-ordered DNA test.

claim: Firodia: the Court's earlier decisions stand against DNA tests being ordered 'on a mere asking', and 'the law does not contemplate use of DNA tests as exploratory or investigatory experiments for determining paternity'.
source: Aparna Ajinkya Firodia v Ajinkya Arun Firodia, 20 Feb 2023 (Nagarathna and Ramasubramanian JJ.), Supreme Court official copy

claim: Dipanwita Roy v Ronobroto Roy (2015) 1 SCC 365, as described in Firodia: the husband made a specific plea of non-access and named the alleged father, so the DNA test was allowed; the wife could decline, and the Court could then draw an adverse inference under Section 114, illustration (h); the Court said a DNA test should be avoided if it can be.
value: DNA test allowed on specific non-access plea
source: Aparna Ajinkya Firodia v Ajinkya Arun Firodia, 20 Feb 2023 (Nagarathna and Ramasubramanian JJ.), Supreme Court official copy
note: Firodia then distinguished Dipanwita Roy: no such specific plea of non-access in Firodia. Year of the Dipanwita Roy decision is not stated in the part read; cite only 'Dipanwita Roy (2015) 1 SCC 365'.

claim: Firodia, Nagarathna J. on the child's rights: genetic information 'goes to the very heart of who he/she is'; children have the right not to have their legitimacy questioned frivolously, which is 'an essential attribute of the right to privacy'; details of parentage are an attribute of a child's identity (the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, Art 8).
source: Aparna Ajinkya Firodia v Ajinkya Arun Firodia, 20 Feb 2023 (Nagarathna and Ramasubramanian JJ.), Supreme Court official copy
note: Quote lengths kept under 15 words each. [Audit 10 Nov 2026] Page corrected: Art 8 CRC passage is on p.43.

claim: Firodia, Ramasubramanian J.: the dispute is between the spouses, not between a spouse and the child, so the child's rights cannot be sacrificed for the husband's fair trial; 'The child cannot be used as a pawn'.
source: Aparna Ajinkya Firodia v Ajinkya Arun Firodia, 20 Feb 2023 (Nagarathna and Ramasubramanian JJ.), Supreme Court official copy

claim: Firodia on Section 114, illustration (h): the Court may presume that a person who refuses to answer, or refuses a test, would have given an unfavourable answer, but s.114 says 'may' and not 'shall'; it is discretionary and should not be applied automatically against a mother who refuses to subject her child to a test.
source: Aparna Ajinkya Firodia v Ajinkya Arun Firodia, 20 Feb 2023 (Nagarathna and Ramasubramanian JJ.), Supreme Court official copy
note: [Audit 10 Nov 2026] Page corrected: the old cite (pp.27 and 70) pointed to Dipanwita Roy extract at p.27; may/shall point is at p.24 and p.70; "not prudent in every case" is p.48.

claim: Section 116 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (Act 47 of 2023, in force 1 Jul 2024) says birth during a valid marriage, or within 280 days after its dissolution with the mother unmarried, is conclusive proof of legitimacy unless the parties had no access to each other when the child could have been begotten.
source: India Code (Legislative Department / MHA), Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, section 116 'Birth during marriage, conclusive proof of legitimacy'
second_source: India Code Act record: assent 25 Dec 2023, enforcement 1-7-2024
note: Read through India Code's data service (indiacode.gov.in/server/api) on 2026-11-10; the section text is the official database text. That it replaces Evidence Act s.112 is shown by the Act's repeal of the 1872 Act (India Code lists the Evidence Act 'Rep., Act 47 of 2023'); the wording matches s.112 as quoted in claim -06 on our reading. Like s.112 it speaks of a person 'born', so it does not reach an unborn child.

claim: PC-PNDT Act, 1994, s.4(2): no pre-natal diagnostic technique shall be conducted except to detect (i) chromosomal abnormalities, (ii) genetic metabolic diseases, (iii) haemoglobinopathies, (iv) sex-linked genetic diseases, (v) congenital anomalies, (vi) others the Central Supervisory Board specifies. s.4(3): only if the qualified person is satisfied, with reasons recorded in writing, of a listed condition (woman over 35; two or more spontaneous abortions or foetal loss; exposure to teratogenic agents; family history of mental retardation or deformity; other). s.4(4): no relative or husband shall seek or encourage a pre-natal test except for the s.4(2) purposes.
value: s.4(2)-(4) restricts pre-natal tests; paternity is not a listed purpose
source: India Code (Ministry of Health and Family Welfare), Pre-conception and Pre-natal Diagnostic Techniques (Prohibition of Sex Selection) Act, 1994 (Act 57 of 1994), s.4 'Regulation of pre-natal diagnostic techniques'
note: Read through India Code's data service on 2026-11-10 (the text includes the 2003 amendment's s.4(3)-(5)). The point that paternity is not a listed purpose is our reading of the closed list; no court has said it. s.4(4) is the clause that reaches a husband or relative who asks for a test.
